questions.prompt: Trace the HRIS login flow from the client's login() to the JWT. Explain when the client falls back to its demo users, how the API finds and checks the account (and why a mixed-case email still works), which claims the token carries and why they matter, which protections and audit records are missing, and the distinction juniors miss here.

keyPoints.text: login() falls back to the local demo users whenever the API call does not return OK, not only when fetch throws.
The API loads the active user including the employee and verifies the password.
keyPoints.quote: Loads active user including employee and verifies password.

keyPoints.text: The API lowercases the submitted email before the lookup, which is why mixed case still works.
The token carries user id, email, role, employee id and employee name.
keyPoints.quote: Emits claims for user id, email, role, employee id, employee name.

keyPoints.text: Those claims must stay aligned with the authorization helpers.
keyPoints.quote: Claims must stay aligned with authorization helpers.

keyPoints.text: There is no lockout or rate limiting.
No audit log is written for login.
keyPoints.quote: No audit log is written for login.

keyPoints.text: Authentication is not the same as authorization.
keyPoints.quote: Authentication is not the same as authorization.

questions.prompt: Trace POST /api/pto for a new PTO request. What does the endpoint validate and reject, whose request it creates and where that identity comes from, what it saves alongside the request and in what initial status, which business checks it does not do, and how the client's demo path differs.

keyPoints.text: The endpoint validates dates and hours, uses the employee id from the claims, and saves the request plus an audit entry.
keyPoints.quote: Validates dates/hours, uses claim employee id, saves request and audit.

keyPoints.text: An end date before the start date, or hours of zero or less, gets a 400.
The client does not decide who the request is for; the API takes employeeId from the claims.
keyPoints.quote: The client does not decide who the request is for

keyPoints.text: A new request starts at manager review.
keyPoints.quote: Default status starts at manager review.

keyPoints.text: It does not check the PTO balance.
Overlapping dates are not checked either.
The client's demo path builds the request locally and bypasses server validation.

questions.prompt: How does GET /api/org-chart build the hierarchy? Explain what it loads and the scale risk, how roots are found, how each node's reports are built and the danger in that recursion, which data shapes still need tests, who may call it, and the invariant the drill asks you to enforce.

keyPoints.text: It loads all employees with department and job role, without tracking.
keyPoints.quote: Loads all employees with department and job role, no tracking.

keyPoints.text: That is an unbounded query for large organizations.
Roots are employees whose ManagerId is null.
ToOrgNode builds each node's reports by filtering the whole flat list again and recursing.
A manager cycle would make that recursion run indefinitely.
Orphaned and cyclic manager data need tests.
Any authenticated user can load the org chart.
keyPoints.quote: Any authenticated user can load org chart

keyPoints.text: The invariant to enforce: no employee can eventually manage themselves.
keyPoints.quote: no employee can eventually manage themselves
